title: Mirabel and the Parish
premise: When a confession letter arrives at coroner Quentin Zhou's office—postmarked the day after Edith Mirabel's funeral—claiming her 'accidental' drowning thirty years ago was murder, Quentin realizes the letter implicates the parish's most beloved founding families, including his own late mother. As he quietly reopens the case, he discovers Edith left him her house and a hidden archive of parish records, making him both heir and investigator. The statute expires in forty days, and someone in the parish will do anything to let it lapse. Quentin must choose between protecting the community that raised him and exposing a truth that will shatter it, ultimately publishing the confession and finding that belonging was never about silence.
about_author: Noor Quintana is the pen name of a former rural journalist who spent a decade covering small-town courts and county fairs across the American Midwest. Their fiction is known for quiet, procedural mysteries steeped in the loyalties and secrets of close-knit communities.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Quentin Zhou's POV. Quentin walks the cemetery after Edith Mirabel's funeral, reciting the dead by name as he always does, and reflects on his three quiet 'corrections' of police verdicts. The parish feels safe, familiar, invisible. Emotional beat: contentment laced with loneliness—the calm before the disruption.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A typed confession arrives claiming Edith's 1994 drowning was murder, postmarked the day after her funeral. No signature, only a parish seal pressed into the paper. Quentin recognizes the paper stock as church stationery. Emotional beat: dread—the intrusion of the past into his ordered world.

chapters.title: The Inheritance Nobody Wanted
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edith's lawyer reads her will: Quentin inherits her crumbling house on Parish Lane, to the visible shock of the Delacroix and Ashford families. Deputy Rosa Vane warns him the police closed the case twice. Emotional beat: unease—he's been seen, claimed, pulled into the parish's web.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Rain
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In Edith's flooded basement he finds her archive: parish newsletters, tide charts, and a ledger of donations with pages razored out. A 1994 newsletter notes Edith witnessed 'an incident at the boathouse' days before she drowned. Emotional beat: the thrill of the hunt shadowed by guilt.

chapters.title: What Rosa Remembers
chapters.summary: Rosa Vane's POV. Rosa, a teenager in 1994, recalls her father, the sheriff, sealing the boathouse records and drinking himself silent. She gives Quentin a box of her father's effects, including a torn photograph of five parish founders at the water's edge. Emotional beat: reluctant complicity turning toward alliance.

chapters.title: The Five Founders
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The photograph shows Edith, Harold Ashford, Celeste Delacroix, Father Ambrose, and Quentin's mother, Lian Zhou. Quentin realizes his mother was there the summer Edith died—and never spoke of it. Emotional beat: betrayal by omission; the case becomes personal.

chapters.title: Ashford's Alibi
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin interviews elderly Harold Ashford at the marina he still owns. Harold's alibi—dinner with the Delacroixs—is airtight, rehearsed, and identical to the version in the 1994 file. Too identical. Emotional beat: cold recognition that the alibi was manufactured.

chapters.title: Celeste's Tea
chapters.summary: Celeste Delacroix's POV. Celeste, the parish's matriarch, serves Quentin tea and deflects with warmth, then privately burns a letter in her study. She knows the confession's author. Emotional beat: the antagonist revealed in miniature—loyalty weaponized into menace.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Ledger
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Cross-referencing tide charts, Quentin proves Edith couldn't have drowned where her body was found; she was moved. The ledger's razored pages match a replacement book still in the church office. Emotional beat: the case shifts from possibility to certainty.

chapters.title: Father Ambrose's Silence
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Dying Father Ambrose, Edith's confessor, hints that Edith came to him the night before she died, 'carrying someone else's sin.' He refuses the seal of confession even now. Emotional beat: the terrible weight of institutional silence.

chapters.title: Lian's Letters
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In Edith's attic, Quentin finds letters from his mother describing a hit-and-run at the boathouse that killed a migrant worker—and the founders' pact to bury it. Edith, the outsider's ally, threatened to expose them. Emotional beat: grief and fury—his mother was a witness who chose the pact.

chapters.title: A Warning on Parish Lane
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Someone ransacks Edith's house and takes the 1994 newsletter. Quentin, warned by a neighbor's glimpse of a parish van, moves the remaining archive to Rosa's. Emotional beat: fear made physical; the investigation is now a target.

chapters.title: Rosa Breaks Rank
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa quietly pulls the sealed boathouse evidence and finds her father's signature on a report dated a day before Edith died—backdated. She copies everything and gives Quentin the original, knowing it ends her career. Emotional beat: loyalty to truth over blood.

chapters.title: The Fourth Grave
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin identifies the migrant worker—Tomás Reyes—in the parish's unmarked section and locates his surviving daughter in the next county. She reveals Edith sent her money every year for thirty years. Emotional beat: the human cost surfaces; guilt becomes grief.

chapters.title: Celeste's Countermove
chapters.summary: Celeste's POV. Celeste convenes the parish council, framing Quentin as a disgraced outsider desecrating Edith's memory. Petitions circulate; his office is audited. Emotional beat: the community turning its face against him—belonging revoked.

chapters.title: The Confession's Hand
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Typewriter forensics on the confession match a machine in the church office—Father Ambrose's. But Ambrose was hospitalized the day it was posted. Someone used his machine and his seal. Emotional beat: a trap within a trap; the author is still hidden.

chapters.title: Harold Confesses to the Wrong Thing
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Confronted, Harold breaks—not about the drowning, but about the pact: he drove the car that hit Tomás, and Celeste orchestrated the cover-up. Edith knew. Emotional beat: the architecture of the lie exposed, one confession short of the murder.

chapters.title: Forty Days, Forty Nights
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. With the statute expiring in a week, Quentin reconstructs the night: Edith confronted Celeste at the boathouse; the drowning was staged as her own accident. The missing piece is physical proof. Emotional beat: desperate clarity against the clock.

chapters.title: The Tide Chart in the Wall
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin finds Edith's final letter sealed in the parish house wall behind the founders' portrait—her eyewitness account of Celeste striking her, plus the razored ledger pages she'd stolen back. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by sorrow; the dead woman speaks at last.

chapters.title: Celeste at the Water
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, then Celeste's. Quentin confronts Celeste at the boathouse with Edith's letter. She neither denies nor apologizes—she offers him the parish's future if he burns it. He refuses. Rosa arrests her as the statute's final hours tick away. Emotional beat: the climax—truth chosen over belonging, at last.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Names
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At a packed parish meeting, Quentin reads Edith's letter aloud and formally names Tomás Reyes in the cemetery records, carving his grave a stone. The parish fractures—some walk out, some stay. Emotional beat: catharsis; the cost of truth made visible and borne.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Months later, Quentin restores Edith's house into a parish archive, Rosa runs for sheriff, and Tomás's daughter visits her father's new stone. Quentin walks the cemetery at dusk, speaking names—including his mother's, forgiven. Emotional beat: belonging rebuilt on truth, not silence.
